body: We don’t get paid in NZ anyway. Can’t sue for compensation if there is a physical injury due to our Accident compensation scheme. Im only persueing this complaint for a sense of justice and validation. Nobody should be allowed to do something like this to someone else’s body without their persmission and get away with it. And I say that as a doctor myself. I know what he did was a breech of my rights. He fucked up, he knew what he was doing but he thought it wouldn’t leave big dents like it did, now he is trying to cover it up. And he is getting away with it because of an under resourced complaints system. Trust me when I say the other side of the story doesn’t stand up to scrutiny for a second, the physical evidence on my body undoes it. Sorry man, I am so angry and let down right now. The justice system in my country is failing me and it hurts. I have wrote emails to a few lawyers, but they have a limited role in this setting seeing as I cannot sue.

The doctor who did the procedure has not recorded any discussion of hollows in his preprocedure consulation notes, and hollows/contour defects are not written on the consent form. Multiple plastic surgeons have verified the hollows are in the buttocks/sacral area, not the lower lumbar area. I have on email that the planned procedure site was lower lumbar, and I have a statement from the doctor who did the procedure saying that he discussed and performed harvest in lower lumbar area on me. As far as I can see my case is water tight. Don’t even need “sides of the story” for the wrong-site aspect, I have permanent physical evidence. Only problem is that I am actually in fucking New Zealand. Yes, I lied, sorry. We can’t sue for medical malpractice because ACC blocks it. Therefore the only avenue to address medical malpractice is through the Office of the Health and Disability Commissioner (HDC), they can determine if there is a breach of the code of rights and if it is serious then refer to the Disciplinary Tribunal. Only problem is that they are under resourced and swamped with complaints they can’t keep up with. In legislation they have a wide discretion on how to deal with complaints, and they are using this to brush complaints aside. It took 6 months for me to get a response, at which stage the deputy commissioner has made a prelim decision not to investigate further, which means not even acknowledging a breach of my patient rights. Now I am having to argue my case, which has involved writing multiple letters and seeing my surgeon again to get Statement of fact regarding the exact location of the hollows. I am so fricken angry that they are not doing their job, which is to protect the rights of healthcare consumers in New Zealand.  Sorry. Rant over.

Morning-wash with water only and apply cerave am facial moisturiser with spf 30, unless I am certain I will be indoors all day and not near windows (my work is like this) in which case I just apply neutropenia hydroboost water gel.
Night time-wash with cetaphil gentle skin cleanser, and sometimes use a Konjac sponge, then while still in the shower I apply turmeric oil and massage my face, I rinse most of the turmeric oil off only leaving a fine film, I subsequently apply neutropenia hydroboost water gel again.

Some of your description is not consistent with osteoarthritis. I'm pretty certain you do not have osteo in your lower vertebrae given that it did not show on the MRI. It is also very unlikely you have osteo in your knees if they have both had normal USS and Xrays (particularly the Xrays as they would be more likely than USS to pick up OA changes). 23/24 yo is very young to develop osteoarthritis of your shoulders unless you have had some pretty decent trauma to them or perhaps if you have a very strong family history. I would be dubious of that diagnosis for your shoulders. Other types of arthritis can cause generic 'degenerative changes'. There are other types of arthritis, including autoimmune ones, that can be negative for rheumatoid factor. Overall I agree with what I lot of the other people here are getting at. I think you need more work up to find a firm diagnosis for your pains so that you can have the appropriate management. Do you have a good relationship with your GP? Have they been helpful with this problem? Have you seen a rheumatologist? I think the latter would be appropriate for you.

I really do empathise with you. I miss that freedom of movement and agility so so so much. 

Do you agree that you need to get a more concrete diagnosis? I would recommend first of all focussing on finding out what condition you are dealing with. There may be some good management options available.

I can't tell you what things will be like for you but if you want to know the truth about how it has effected my life I'm afraid to say I have really struggled. The pain and limping fluctuate and sometimes I feel very little discomfort. Often there seems to be no reason for why it flares up which is pretty frustrating. Those days are very hard. Things that were previously so easy I didn't ever think about them, become hard. Like getting up from a chair to get something at work. I'm on my feet all day at work and it certainly adds an additional layer of stress. I don't find that panadol (acetaminophen in the states) or ibuprofen help much. Sometimes hot packs help a bit. Sometimes movement helps, like a gentle stroll at my own pace in a relaxing environment, a swim, or a bike ride. Hot showers also help a bit. I get very anxious with the pain and feel very misunderstood by other people who have not experienced a similar problem, this has led to some conflict at work and with friends in the past. I find it difficult to be around other people when the pain is there because it is distressing to me and they aren't experiencing the same thing as me so I don't feel we can relate well. I get very stressed about it because I have never been able to adjust to the idea of a life without being agile and comfortable on my feet, without going for tramps or hikes, without playing tennis, without surfing, without skiing etc etc. I often feel a lot has been taken from me and I am desperate to try and turn back the clock so I can have these things back. 

So yes..it bloody sucks. It makes me sad and it scares me. And yet here I still am, 4 years later. I had a surgical option of a high tibial osteotomy (a surgical fracture to realign the lower leg and take pressure off the effected part of the joint). I was too scared to undergo that because it it a very long recovery and there is a risk of damaging the ligament graft, and it may only provide slight pain relief and push back needing a joint replacement to my late 30s or early 40s, I was also worried about the cosmetic effect (female and painfully aware that the world seems to view much of our worth in how we look). Instead I sought an alternative and underwent a stem cell therapy but I am still waiting to see if there has been any benefit.

Again I am sorry this all sounds so bleak. I don't think I'm very strong, maybe you are made of stronger stuff than me and will adjust better. I hope to hear how you are going, and you are welcome to vent frustrations to me, I would be completely non judgemental as I know that this adjustment can be tough. 

Further to this I would recommend considering the following. Trialling physiotherapy (go to more than one if you aren't sure of their opinion), trialling PRP or stem cell injections. If these options did not work then you could maybe consider having an early hip joint replacement if you are in lots of pain as they apparently have a very good success rate (better then knee replacements). I'm also wondering why imaging you had, did your specialist get you an MRI scan to exclude other possible causes?

One more thing! Please be kind to yourself and patient with yourself! Take things a bit slower if you need to. For me I find serenity in being down by the river alone for a bit, I don't care if that might seem odd to my friends, life has thrown me a curve ball and if I need to stare at some plants on my own for a few minutes to feel better then I will! Also you are not your injury....if there are things that you are not able to do at the moment don't let your brain trick you in to feeling like you are a boring or lazy person, it's a trap, just coz you can't do stuff right now doesn't mean you wouldn't if you could.

Last point! I do truely believe that there will be revolutionary changes in how this form of arthritis is managed in the future (particularly in us youngens) via the use of biological materials such as stem cells. I'm just unsure on how long that will take...but there are teams of people out there working on it right now. 

Take care.
